results.name: Schur complement elimination and inverse
results.statement: Let K be a field, p and q nonnegative integers, A in K^(p×p), B in K^(p×q), C in K^(q×p), and D in K^(q×q). Assume A is invertible. Set S=D−CA⁻¹B and M=[[A,B],[C,D]]. Then M is invertible if and only if S is invertible. In that case M⁻¹=[[A⁻¹+A⁻¹BS⁻¹CA⁻¹,−A⁻¹BS⁻¹],[−S⁻¹CA⁻¹,S⁻¹]]. The equation M(x,y)=(f,g) reduces to Sy=g−CA⁻¹f and x=A⁻¹(f−By).
hypotheses: K is a commutative field. All block products have the stated dimensions.
A has a two-sided inverse. The inverse formula requires a two-sided inverse of S.

definitions.name: matrix inverse
definitions.text: An inverse N of M satisfies MN=NM=I.

definitions.name: Schur complement
definitions.text: For an invertible A, the Schur complement of A in M is S=D−CA⁻¹B.

/-- LDU decomposition of a block matrix with an invertible top-left corner, using the
Schur complement. -/
theorem fromBlocks_eq_of_invertible₁₁ (A : Matrix m m α) (B : Matrix m n α) (C : Matrix l m α)
    (D : Matrix l n α) [Invertible A] :
    fromBlocks A B C D =
      fromBlocks 1 0 (C * ⅟A) 1 * fromBlocks A 0 0 (D - C * ⅟A * B) *
        fromBlocks 1 (⅟A * B) 0 1 := by
  simp only [fromBlocks_multiply, Matrix.mul_zero, Matrix.zero_mul, add_zero, zero_add,
    Matrix.one_mul, Matrix.mul_one, invOf_mul_self, Matrix.mul_invOf_cancel_left,
    Matrix.mul_assoc, add_sub_cancel]

theorem invOf_fromBlocks₁₁_eq (A : Matrix m m α) (B : Matrix m n α) (C : Matrix n m α)
    (D : Matrix n n α) [Invertible A] [Invertible (D - C * ⅟A * B)]
    [Invertible (fromBlocks A B C D)] :
    ⅟(fromBlocks A B C D) =
      fromBlocks (⅟A + ⅟A * B * ⅟(D - C * ⅟A * B) * C * ⅟A) (-(⅟A * B * ⅟(D - C * ⅟A * B)))
        (-(⅟(D - C * ⅟A * B) * C * ⅟A)) (⅟(D - C * ⅟A * B)) := by
  let := fromBlocks₁₁Invertible A B C D
  convert (rfl : ⅟(fromBlocks A B C D) = _)

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Define L=[[I,0],[CA⁻¹,I]], H=[[A,0],[0,S]], and U=[[I,A⁻¹B],[0,I]]. Direct block multiplication gives LH=[[A,0],[C,S]]. Therefore LHU=[[A,B],[C,CA⁻¹B+S]]=M.
The matrices L and U have inverses L⁻¹=[[I,0],[−CA⁻¹,I]] and U⁻¹=[[I,−A⁻¹B],[0,I]]. Multiply each proposed inverse on both sides to obtain the identity. No inverse of S enters these products.
If S is invertible, then H⁻¹=[[A⁻¹,0],[0,S⁻¹]]. Both HH⁻¹ and H⁻¹H equal the identity. Thus U⁻¹H⁻¹L⁻¹ is a two-sided inverse of LHU=M.
If M is invertible, then H=L⁻¹MU⁻¹ is invertible, with inverse UM⁻¹L. Write its inverse as [[E,F],[G,J]]. The bottom-right blocks of HH⁻¹=I and H⁻¹H=I give SJ=JS=I. Thus S is invertible.
Multiply U⁻¹H⁻¹ to obtain [[A⁻¹,−A⁻¹BS⁻¹],[0,S⁻¹]]. Its product with L⁻¹ is the displayed inverse. The order of every factor matters. No interchange of matrix factors occurs.

The first block equation is Ax+By=f. Since A is invertible, x=A⁻¹(f−By). Substitute this into Cx+Dy=g to obtain Sy=g−CA⁻¹f. Conversely these two reduced equations imply both original equations. Empty blocks satisfy the same identities.

worked_application.title: A saddle-point system without a full inverse
hypotheses: The entries lie in ℝ. A=diag(2,3), B=(1,1)ᵀ, C=(1,1), and D=0.
A is invertible because 2 and 3 are nonzero.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The Schur complement reduces 3 equations to 1 scalar equation. Its nonzero value also proves that the full matrix is invertible.

steps.text: Compute A⁻¹=diag(1/2,1/3). Then S=0−(1,1)diag(1/2,1/3)(1,1)ᵀ=−5/6. Thus S has inverse −6/5.
For f=(1,2)ᵀ and g=0, the reduced right side is g−CA⁻¹f=−(1/2+2/3)=−7/6. Therefore y=(−6/5)(−7/6)=7/5.
Check the original equations. The values give 2(−1/5)+7/5=1, 3(1/5)+7/5=2, and −1/5+1/5=0. The solution is unique because A and S are invertible.

results.name: Operator Neumann series with a certified truncation error
results.statement: Let E be a Banach space over ℝ or ℂ. Let T:E→E be a bounded linear operator with q=‖T‖<1. Then I−T has bounded inverse R=∑_{n=0}^∞ Tⁿ, where the series converges in operator norm. For every integer N≥0, ‖R−∑_{n=0}^N Tⁿ‖≤q^(N+1)/(1−q), and ‖R‖≤1/(1−q).
hypotheses: E is complete for its norm. T is linear and bounded.
The operator norm satisfies q=‖T‖<1. N is an integer with N≥0.

prerequisites.reason: The scalar series ∑qⁿ converges to 1/(1−q) for 0≤q<1. This bounds every operator tail.
The worked application integrates continuous polynomial and exponential functions through their antiderivatives.

definitions.name: operator norm
definitions.text: ‖T‖ is the least bound c≥0 for which ‖Tx‖≤c‖x‖ for all x.

definitions.name: Banach space
definitions.text: A Banach space is a normed real or complex vector space in which every Cauchy sequence converges.

definitions.name: operator series
definitions.text: Convergence in operator norm means that the operator norms of the differences of partial sums and the limit tend to 0.

theorem IsUnit.one_sub_of_norm_lt_one {x : R} (hx : ‖x‖ < 1) : IsUnit (1 - x) :=
  hasSummableGeomSeries_iff_isUnit.mp inferInstance hx

lemma summable_geometric_of_norm_lt_one {x : R} (h : ‖x‖ < 1) : Summable (fun n ↦ x ^ n) :=
  hasSummableGeomSeries_iff_summable_pow.mp inferInstance h

theorem geom_series_mul_neg (x : R) (h : ‖x‖ < 1) : (∑' i : ℕ, x ^ i) * (1 - x) = 1 :=
  (summable_geometric_of_norm_lt_one h).tsum_pow_mul_one_sub

theorem mul_neg_geom_series (x : R) (h : ‖x‖ < 1) : (1 - x) * ∑' i : ℕ, x ^ i = 1 :=
  (summable_geometric_of_norm_lt_one h).one_sub_mul_tsum_pow

source.alignment: The source proves invertibility and both inverse equations in a normed ring with summable geometric series. The authored proof treats bounded operators on a Banach space and proves the quantitative tail estimate.

results.proof_status: source proof inspected; authored proof awaits inference review; no local Lean check

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: For bounded operators U and V, ‖UVx‖≤‖U‖‖V‖‖x‖. Thus ‖UV‖≤‖U‖‖V‖. Induction gives ‖Tⁿ‖≤qⁿ for n≥1. Also ‖I‖≤1, including the zero space.

Let P_N=∑_{n=0}^N Tⁿ. For m>N, the triangle inequality gives ‖P_m−P_N‖≤∑_{n=N+1}^m qⁿ≤q^(N+1)/(1−q). The linked scalar geometric series proves that this bound tends to 0. Hence the partial sums form a Cauchy sequence in operator norm.

For each x, the sequence P_Nx is Cauchy because ‖(P_m−P_N)x‖≤‖P_m−P_N‖‖x‖. Completeness of E gives a limit Rx. Limits preserve addition and scalar multiplication, so R is linear. The bound ‖P_Nx‖≤(∑_{n=0}^N qⁿ)‖x‖ gives ‖Rx‖≤‖x‖/(1−q). Thus R is bounded.

For every x, take m→∞ in the tail estimate to obtain ‖(R−P_N)x‖≤q^(N+1)‖x‖/(1−q). Continuity of the norm follows from |‖u‖−‖v‖|≤‖u−v‖. The definition of operator norm gives the stated tail bound and proves P_N→R in operator norm.

Finite cancellation gives (I−T)P_N=P_N(I−T)=I−T^(N+1). The operator norm of T^(N+1) is at most q^(N+1), which tends to 0. Products with the fixed bounded operator I−T preserve operator-norm limits by the first-step bound. Therefore (I−T)R=R(I−T)=I.
The tail and inverse bounds also hold when q=0. In that case T=0, R=I, and every tail is 0. The proof does not require different operators to commute. It uses only powers of T.

worked_application.title: A quantitative Volterra integral equation
worked_application.goal: Solve u(x)−(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt=1 for x in [0,1], and bound a finite approximation.
hypotheses: E=C([0,1],ℝ) with the uniform norm is complete.
Define (Tu)(x)=(1/2)∫₀ˣu(t)dt. This operator is linear and maps continuous functions to continuous functions.

Completeness follows directly: a uniform Cauchy sequence has pointwise real limits. The same Cauchy estimate proves uniform convergence. For a point x, select one continuous approximant within ε/3 of the limit. Its continuity and the triangle inequality prove continuity of the limit at x.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The uniform estimate gives ‖T‖≤1/2<1. The Neumann theorem gives uniqueness and a uniform error bound for successive integral approximations.

steps.text: For ‖u‖∞≤1, |(Tu)(x)|≤x/2≤1/2. The function u=1 attains 1/2 at x=1. Thus ‖T‖=1/2.
Induct on n. The case n=0 gives T⁰1=1=x⁰/(2⁰0!). Integrate xⁿ/(2ⁿn!) to obtain T^(n+1)1=x^(n+1)/(2^(n+1)(n+1)!).

The inverse yields u(x)=∑_{n=0}^∞ xⁿ/(2ⁿn!). Define exp(s) by its real power series. This gives u(x)=exp(x/2). The ratio of consecutive absolute terms is at most 1/(2(n+1)) on [0,1], so the series converges uniformly. An integral of a uniform error is at most that error times the interval length. Thus the integral preserves this series limit.
Use N=6. The approximation u₆(x)=∑_{n=0}^6 xⁿ/(2ⁿn!) satisfies ‖u−u₆‖∞≤(1/2)^7/(1−1/2)=1/64. At x=1 it gives u₆(1)=75973/46080. The exact value is exp(1/2).
Check the equation directly: (1/2)∫₀ˣexp(t/2)dt=exp(x/2)−1. Thus u−Tu=1. The inverse theorem proves that no other continuous solution exists.

worked_application.result: The unique solution is u(x)=exp(x/2). The degree-6 approximation has uniform error at most 1/64.

limitations: The sufficient condition ‖T‖<1 is not necessary for invertibility.
The proof requires completeness. The bound is in operator norm, not an entrywise norm.

results.name: Finite-field Gauss sum magnitude and quadratic square
results.statement: Let F be a finite field of q elements. Let χ:F×→ℂ× be a nontrivial multiplicative character, extended by χ(0)=0. Let ψ:(F,+)→ℂ× be a nontrivial additive character. Define G(χ,ψ)=∑_{x∈F}χ(x)ψ(x). Then |G(χ,ψ)|²=q. If χ²=1 on F×, then G(χ,ψ)²=χ(−1)q.
hypotheses: F is a field with finitely many elements. q=|F|.
χ and ψ are group homomorphisms to nonzero complex numbers. Neither character is trivial.
The square formula requires χ(x)²=1 for every nonzero x.

prerequisites.reason: The worked application constructs the additive character from a primitive fifth root through de Moivre’s formula.

definitions.name: multiplicative character
definitions.text: χ(xy)=χ(x)χ(y) for nonzero field elements, and χ(1)=1. Extend χ to 0 by χ(0)=0.

definitions.name: additive character
definitions.text: ψ(x+y)=ψ(x)ψ(y), and ψ(0)=1. Nontrivial means ψ(z)≠1 for some z.

definitions.name: Gauss sum
definitions.text: G(χ,ψ)=∑_{x∈F}χ(x)ψ(x). The sum includes 0, whose term is 0.

source.excerpt:
/-- We have `gaussSum χ ψ * gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ⁻¹ = Fintype.card R`
when `χ` is nontrivial and `ψ` is primitive (and `R` is a field). -/
theorem gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card {χ : MulChar R R'} (hχ : χ ≠ 1) {ψ : AddChar R R'}
    (hψ : IsPrimitive ψ) :
    gaussSum χ ψ * gaussSum χ⁻¹ ψ⁻¹ = Fintype.card R := by
  simp only [gaussSum, AddChar.inv_apply, Finset.sum_mul, Finset.mul_sum, MulChar.inv_apply']
  conv =>
    enter [1, 2, x, 2, y]
    rw [mul_mul_mul_comm, ← map_mul, ← map_add_eq_mul, ← sub_eq_add_neg]
--  conv in _ * _ * (_ * _) => rw [mul_mul_mul_comm, ← map_mul, ← map_add_eq_mul, ← sub_eq_add_neg]
  simp_rw [gaussSum_mul_aux hχ ψ]
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  classical -- to get `[DecidableEq R]` for `sum_mulShift`
  simp_rw [← Finset.mul_sum, sum_mulShift _ hψ, sub_eq_zero, apply_ite, Nat.cast_zero, mul_zero]
  rw [Finset.sum_ite_eq' Finset.univ (1 : R)]
  simp only [Finset.mem_univ, map_one, one_mul, ite_true]

source_references.excerpt:
/-- When `χ` is a nontrivial quadratic character, then the square of `gaussSum χ ψ`
is `χ(-1)` times the cardinality of `R`. -/
theorem gaussSum_sq {χ : MulChar R R'} (hχ₁ : χ ≠ 1) (hχ₂ : IsQuadratic χ)
    {ψ : AddChar R R'} (hψ : IsPrimitive ψ) :
    gaussSum χ ψ ^ 2 = χ (-1) * Fintype.card R := by
  rw [pow_two, ← gaussSum_mul_gaussSum_eq_card hχ₁ hψ, hχ₂.inv, mul_rotate']
  congr
  rw [mul_comm, ← gaussSum_mulShift _ _ (-1 : Rˣ), inv_mulShift]
  rfl

proof.scope: The full statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Every nonzero character value has finite multiplicative order because its source group is finite. Thus |χ(x)|=1 for x≠0 and |ψ(x)|=1 for all x. Their complex conjugates equal their inverses.
Choose a∈F× with χ(a)≠1. The bijection x↦ax on F× shows ∑_{x∈F×}χ(x)=χ(a)∑_{x∈F×}χ(x). Subtract the two sides and divide by 1−χ(a). Therefore the multiplicative character sum is 0.

Choose z∈F with ψ(z)≠1. The bijection x↦x+z gives ∑_{x∈F}ψ(x)=ψ(z)∑_{x∈F}ψ(x), so this additive character sum is 0. If b≠0, multiplication by b permutes F. Hence ∑_{y∈F}ψ(by)=0. Remove the y=0 term to obtain ∑_{y∈F×}ψ(by)=−1. For b=0 the latter sum is q−1.

Expand |G|²=G conjugate(G) as a finite double sum. Terms with x=0 or y=0 vanish. For each y≠0, write x=ty. This bijection changes χ(x)conjugate(χ(y)) to χ(t), and ψ(x)conjugate(ψ(y)) to ψ((t−1)y). Thus |G|²=∑_{t∈F×}χ(t)∑_{y∈F×}ψ((t−1)y).
Separate t=1. Its inner sum is q−1 and χ(1)=1. Every other t contributes −χ(t). The zero sum in step 2 gives ∑_{t≠0,1}χ(t)=−1. Therefore |G|²=(q−1)−(−1)=q.

If χ²=1 on F×, all its values are real and equal to 1 or −1. Therefore conjugate(G)=∑χ(x)ψ(−x). Replace x by −x to obtain conjugate(G)=χ(−1)G. Since χ(−1)²=1, the magnitude equation yields χ(−1)G²=q, or G²=χ(−1)q.

worked_application.title: Exact quadratic exponential sums modulo 5
worked_application.goal: Compute ∑_{x=0}^4 exp(2πiax²/5) for a=1 and a=2.
hypotheses: F=ℤ/5ℤ is a field. Put ζ=exp(2πi/5) and ψ(t)=ζᵗ.
Define χ(1)=χ(4)=1 and χ(2)=χ(3)=−1. Extend χ(0)=0.
worked_application.why_theorem_applies: The Gauss theorem fixes the magnitude and square of an oscillatory sum. A sign check then gives an exact value.

steps.text: The element 2 generates F×. Its successive powers are 1,2,4,3, with χ-values 1,−1,1,−1. Thus χ is a nontrivial homomorphism. By de Moivre’s formula, ζ=cos(2π/5)+i sin(2π/5) satisfies ζ⁵=1. Its angle shows ζ≠1. Hence ψ(t)=ζᵗ is a well-defined nontrivial additive character.
The squares x² for x=0,1,2,3,4 are 0,1,4,4,1. Thus the number of roots of x²=t is 1+χ(t) for each t in F. For a≠0, the additive-character sum ∑_tψ(at) is 0. Therefore S(a)=∑_tχ(t)ψ(at).
Replace t by a⁻¹s to obtain S(a)=χ(a)⁻¹G. Here χ(a)⁻¹=χ(a), so S(1)=G and S(2)=−G.
Since χ(−1)=χ(4)=1, the theorem gives G²=5. Directly G=ζ+ζ⁴−ζ²−ζ³=2cos(2π/5)−2cos(4π/5). The first cosine is positive and the second is negative. Hence G>0 and G=√5.
Thus S(1)=√5 and S(2)=−√5. Direct enumeration also gives S(1)=1+2ζ+2ζ⁴ and S(2)=1+2ζ²+2ζ³. The identity 1+ζ+ζ²+ζ³+ζ⁴=0 makes these expressions agree with the Gauss calculation.

worked_application.result: The sums are √5 for a=1 and −√5 for a=2. The square formula alone does not select the sign.
worked_application.verification: Authored calculation; mathematical review remains pending.

limitations: Neither character may be trivial. The proof requires a field, not an arbitrary finite ring.
The quadratic square formula does not determine the sign of G. A further argument must select the square root.
